THOUGHT: This 18-month-old boy presents with acute, spontaneous right knee swelling (hemarthrosis confirmed on ultrasound) without history of trauma. The absence of trauma in a toddler—especially one who is just beginning to walk and play actively—makes traumatic hemarthrosis unlikely unless the injury was severe, yet parents report no such event. The warmth without erythema or fever makes septic arthritis less likely, and the normal WBC and lack of systemic symptoms (no fever, rash, illness) further argue against infection or inflammatory arthritis. The coagulation testing reveals a prolonged activated clotting time (ACT = 52 s), while PT is normal (14 s) and thrombin time is normal — this pattern suggests an intrinsic pathway defect (e.g., factor VIII, IX, or XI deficiency), not vitamin K deficiency or liver disease (which would prolong PT/INR). Factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A) is X-linked recessive; the maternal uncle with “similar problems” strongly supports an X-linked bleeding disorder in the maternal lineage. Hemophilia A is the most common inherited coagulopathy presenting with hemarthrosis in early childhood, especially in males. The age (18 months) aligns with onset of ambulation and increased joint stress, triggering first recognized bleeds. CBC shows normal Hb and platelets, ruling out thrombocytopenia or anemia from chronic blood loss. Reticulocyte count is normal, arguing against acute hemorrhage-induced compensatory erythropoiesis. Thus, the constellation — spontaneous hemarthrosis, X-linked family history, isolated intrinsic pathway abnormality (prolonged ACT, normal PT/TT) — points overwhelmingly to hemophilia A.

DIAGNOSIS: Hemophilia A
